```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4,
                      dpi = 150)
library(SIGA)
vig_dir <- file.path("..", "vignettes")
## Body of a vignette without its YAML header and set-up chunk.
vignette_body <- function(file) {
  x <- readLines(file.path(vig_dir, file), encoding = "UTF-8")
  dashes <- which(x == "---")
  x <- x[-seq_len(dashes[2])]
  start <- grep("^```\\{r, include = FALSE\\}", x)
  if (length(start)) {
    end <- which(x == "```" & seq_along(x) > start[1])[1]
    x <- x[-(start[1]:end)]
  }
  x <- x[!grepl("^library\\(SIGA\\)$", x)]
  x <- sub("^(#+) [0-9]+\\. ", "\\1 ", x)   # the manual numbers sections itself
  paste(x, collapse = "\n")
}
child <- function(file) {
  cat(knitr::knit_child(text = vignette_body(file), quiet = TRUE, envir = globalenv()))
}
```

# Introduction

SIGA (*subgroup identification based on a genetic algorithm*) is a method for
finding, in the data of a two-arm randomised clinical trial, a subgroup of
patients defined by a combination of biomarker conditions in which the
treatment effect is much larger than in the remaining patients. It was
proposed for censored survival data by Zhao et al. (2024,
*Journal of Biopharmaceutical Statistics* 34(1), 55–77,
doi:10.1080/10543406.2023.2170397) and is extended in this package to binary
and continuous endpoints.

Compared with tree-based methods, which split the population one biomarker
at a time, the genetic algorithm evaluates complete subgroup definitions, so
that several biomarkers that are only predictive in combination can be found
together. Because any search will find a "best" subgroup even in the absence
of a real effect, SIGA embeds the search in a resampling scheme that controls

* **multiplicity**: a subgroup is reported only if the subgroups found in
  random training subsamples also improve the treatment effect in the held-out
  patients by at least $100\eta\%$; and
* **complexity**: only biomarkers that are selected in at least a proportion
  $\theta$ of the resamples can define the subgroup.

The package provides:

* `siga()`, the complete procedure, with print, summary, plot and prediction
  methods, and `update()` to change $\eta$ and $\theta$ without recomputation;
* `siga_search()`, the genetic algorithm search on given biomarkers;
* `siga_screen()`, the prescreening of candidate biomarkers;
* `siga_cv()`, cross-validation of the complete procedure;
* `subgroup_effect()`, the treatment effects in a subgroup, its complement and
  the interaction, e.g. in validation data;
* `siga_simulate()`, data from the simulation models of the SIGA paper.

```{r flowchart, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 5.2, fig.cap = "The SIGA procedure."}

# Installation

SIGA depends on the genetic algorithm toolbox **gatbxr** (version 0.2.0 or
later), and on **survival** and **mvtnorm** from CRAN. Until both packages are
on CRAN they are installed from GitHub:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("drizztxx/gatbxr")
remotes::install_github("drizztxx/SIGA", build_vignettes = TRUE)
```

The optional package **randomForestSRC** enables the random forest
prescreening (`screen = "rf"`). Parallel computing (`n_cores > 1`) uses the
**parallel** package that comes with R; it works on all operating systems,
including Windows. The vignettes reproduce the chapters of this manual:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
browseVignettes("SIGA")
```

# Function reference

| Function | Purpose | Main arguments |
|---|---|---|
| `siga()` | complete SIGA procedure | `formula`, `data`, `control_arm`, `direction`, `eta`, `theta`, `n_resample`, `resample_subpop`, `screen`, `n_candidates`, `control`, `n_cores`, `seed` |
| `update()` | new `eta` / `theta` for a `siga` fit | `object`, `eta`, `theta` |
| `siga_search()` | genetic algorithm search only | `formula`, `data`, `control`, `n_cores`, `seed` |
| `siga_screen()` | prescreening of candidate biomarkers | `formula`, `data`, `method`, `n_candidates` |
| `siga_control()` | genetic algorithm settings | `pop_size`, `max_gen`, `n_subpop`, `ggap`, `min_size`, `objective` |
| `siga_cv()` | k-fold cross-validation | `formula`, `data`, `k`, `repeats`, `...` (passed to `siga()`) |
| `subgroup_effect()` | effects in subgroup and complement | `object`, `data` |
| `predict()` | subgroup membership | `object`, `newdata` |
| `plot()` | `"frequency"`, `"resamples"`, `"convergence"`, `"effect"` | `x`, `type` |
| `summary()`, `print()` | reports | |
| `format()`, `rule_members()`, `rule_variables()` | subgroup rules | `x`, `style`, `digits`, `data` |
| `siga_simulate()` | data from the simulation models of the paper | `n`, `model`, `endpoint`, `n_noise`, `legacy`, `seed` |
| `siga_true_subgroup()` | true subgroup of the simulation models | `data`, `model` |

The formula has the form `outcome ~ treatment | predictors`: the outcome is
`Surv(time, status)`, a binary variable or a numeric variable; the treatment
variable has two values (`control_arm` sets the control); the predictors are
column names separated by `+`, or `.` for all remaining columns. The help
pages (e.g. `?siga`) document every argument and returned component.

**Output of `siga()`.** The fit contains, among others, `subgroup` (was a
subgroup identified?), `rule` (the subgroup), `decision` (mean held-out effect
ratio, threshold, selected biomarkers and the reason for "no subgroup"),
`resamples` (one row per resample), `frequency` (selection frequency of every
biomarker), `screening` (prescreening of the complete data), `final` (the
final search, including the best subgroup of each sub-population) and
`effects` (treatment effects in the subgroup and its complement).
